title: Rosi Braidotti
summary: Rosi Braidotti (b. 1954) is an Italian-Australian philosopher working in the Netherlands, an heir to Spinoza and Deleuze, and one of the leading theorists of posthumanism and feminism. She invites us to see the human being not as a separate master of nature but as a "nomadic subject" — a moving knot of connections with other people, animals, technologies and the planet.
onEmotions: Braidotti thinks about feelings through Spinoza and Deleuze: affects are what increase or decrease our capacity to act and to connect with the world (she calls this capacity potentia). She doesn't divide emotions into "good" and "bad" in a moral sense, but she distinguishes forces that drain us from forces that affirm life. Her "affirmative" ethics doesn't demand positive thinking and doesn't deny pain: it is about slowly, together with others, transforming passive suffering into an active force. For Braidotti, a person is a "nomadic subject", always in motion and in connection, so feelings never belong to them alone.

anxiety.text: Anxiety today is a very understandable feeling. Rosi Braidotti describes our time as a point where several great transformations converge at once: the rapid development of technology and an ecological crisis that threatens countless forms of life. Braidotti doesn't pretend this isn't frightening. But she offers a particular way of relating to such a state — "cartography": not trying to take in everything at once, but honestly mapping where you are, what is acting on you and what you are connected to. Anxiety feeds on vagueness; a map gives you back something concrete. Seen this way, your anxiety is sensitivity to the real world, not a malfunction. It can become a point of orientation: a way of noticing what in your situation truly depends on you, and who you are not alone with in it.
anxiety.practice: Draw a small "map" of your anxiety: you in the centre, and around you three things that weigh on you and three that support you.

fear.text: Fear is a natural protection, and it deserves respect. Rosi Braidotti, following Spinoza and Deleuze, says that every body has its own "thresholds of sustainability" — limits to how much it can bear without breaking down. Fear often signals that you have come close to such a threshold. From this point of view, fear is not cowardice but knowledge about the limits of your strength. Braidotti also stresses that these thresholds aren't fixed once and for all: they widen when we are held by connections and narrow in isolation. So the point is not to heroically ignore fear, but to respect your limits and, gradually and in the company of others, expand what you are able to bear.
fear.practice: Ask yourself: what threshold is this fear bringing me to? What or who could help me feel steadier next to it?

sadness.text: There's no need to be ashamed of sadness — it is part of life. Rosi Braidotti draws on Spinoza, for whom sadness is the experience of our capacity to act and feel being diminished. Braidotti calls this capacity potentia — power as ability, as opposed to potestas, power as domination over others. By this logic, sadness is not a moral failure but an honest sense that, for a while, you have less strength. Braidotti's affirmative ethics doesn't ask you to pretend everything is fine. It asks a different question: which connections and encounters could gradually give you back your strength? In this light, sadness is not a dead end but a state you can pass through — especially if you don't stay in it alone.
sadness.practice: What kind of encounter — with a person, a place, a book, an animal — usually gives you even a little more strength? Could you arrange a small encounter like that today?

grief.text: Grief is an enormous pain, and no philosophy should explain it away. Rosi Braidotti insists on this: her affirmative ethics is not about denying suffering, nor about positive thinking. It is about the slow transformation of pain — about finding, over time and together with others, a way to go on living within it and to stay connected to the world. Braidotti is fond of the word "endurance", which holds both meanings: to bear and to last. Grief asks exactly this of us — not victory, but the ability to go on lasting alongside the pain. From this point of view, one could say that your bond with what you have lost does not vanish: it keeps changing you and becomes part of who you are becoming. The love that was remains an active force.
grief.practice: What of who this person was to you — or of what you have lost — lives on in your habits, your words, your values? Name one thing.

loneliness.text: Loneliness hurts, and it is the natural pain of a being made for connection. Rosi Braidotti describes the human being as a "nomadic subject" — not a closed-off unit but a moving knot of relations with other people, animals, places, technologies, the planet itself. Even when no one is around, these connections don't disappear entirely: you are held by the air you breathe, by food someone grew, by a language shaped over generations. At the same time, Braidotti doesn't erase differences: our experiences are not the same, and loneliness can come from your particularity going unseen. Seen this way, loneliness is not a sign that you are cut off from the world, but a longing for connections where you will be accepted in your difference. Such connections are possible precisely because togetherness doesn't require sameness.
loneliness.practice: Name three non-human connections that are holding you right now — for instance, the tree outside the window, a cup of tea, familiar music.

quote.text: We are in this together, but we are not one and the same.
quote.author: Rosi Braidotti

anger.text: Anger is a legitimate feeling, especially in the face of injustice. Rosi Braidotti, after Nietzsche and Deleuze, distinguishes between "reactive" and "affirmative" forces. Reactive anger gets stuck in grievance: it returns to the wound again and again and keeps us tied to what hurt us. Braidotti doesn't condemn this kind of anger, but she shows that over time it drains us. The affirmative path is not to suppress anger but to transform its energy — to turn it into a force for creating, protecting, building different connections. From this point of view, your anger is a valuable signal and a powerful charge. The question is not whether it is "right" to be angry, but where you want to direct this force so that it works for you rather than against you.
anger.practice: If the energy of your anger could be channelled into something creative, what would it be? Write down one idea, however small.

shame.text: Shame makes you shrink: it feels as though you don't measure up to what a person is supposed to be. Rosi Braidotti shows that this "proper human" is itself a historical construction. The classical humanist ideal — embodied, for instance, in Leonardo's Vitruvian Man — quietly assumed a particular norm: male, European, healthy and able-bodied. Everything that differed from it was treated as deviation. Braidotti proposes a posthuman view in which difference is not a flaw but a feature of life. For her the subject is "nomadic" — always in process, never frozen. Seen this way, shame tries to fix you in a single image: "I am bad." But you are not a finished portrait; you are movement. The way you don't fit the norm may simply be your way of being alive.
shame.practice: Finish the sentence: "I feel ashamed because I don't fit the norm of…". Then ask: who invented this norm, and when?

guilt.text: Guilt can be honest when you really have hurt someone. Rosi Braidotti, following Nietzsche and Deleuze, is wary of a culture of guilt that keeps people in constant self-accusation and paralyses them. Instead, she speaks of accountability — the ability to recognise your place in a web of connections and how your actions affect it. The difference is subtle but important: guilt looks backwards and asks "how bad am I?", while accountability looks forward and asks "what can be done now?". From this point of view, your guilt can become a starting point not for punishing yourself, but for action that repairs connections and makes the world a little better.
guilt.practice: Reframe your guilt as a question of accountability: not "how guilty am I?" but "what one step can I take now?".

envy.text: Envy is an unpleasant but very understandable feeling. Braidotti doesn't write about envy directly, but her distinction between two kinds of power sheds a lot of light on it. Potestas is power as domination: status, position, a place in the hierarchy. There is never enough of it to go round, and people have to compete for it. Potentia is power as capacity: the ability to act, feel, create, connect with others. It grows when it is shared. From Braidotti's point of view, one could say that envy is almost always looking at potestas: the other person seems to have more room, recognition, success. But what makes life truly rich lies in the realm of potentia, and someone else's success doesn't take it away from you. You might ask yourself: what capacity — rather than status — do I actually want to develop?
envy.practice: Look at the object of your envy and ask: is there a desire for status behind it, or a desire to be able to do, feel or create something? Write down one word.

emptiness.text: Emptiness can be a heavy state: it feels as though nothing inside is moving. Rosi Braidotti invites us to look at life more broadly than our personal experiences. She speaks of zoe — the vital force that runs through everything alive, not only through humans: through plants, animals, the cells of our bodies. Zoe doesn't ask whether we're in the mood right now — it simply keeps working: the heart beats, the breath goes on, the body repairs itself. From this point of view, one could say that your "self" may feel empty, but life in you doesn't stop. This isn't a demand to "cheer up" but a quiet support: you don't have to produce all the meaning on your own. Sometimes it's enough just to be near something that lives — a plant, an animal, the sky.
emptiness.practice: Spend a minute near something alive — a plant, an animal, your own breathing. Simply notice: life goes on in you, too.

confusion.text: Confusion is frightening, but for Rosi Braidotti it is almost the natural state of the contemporary person. Her "nomadic subject" lives in motion, without an identity fixed once and for all. Drawing on Deleuze and Foucault, Braidotti offers an important distinction: the actual — what we are ceasing to be — and the virtual — what we are becoming. Confusion often arises exactly at this seam: the old self is already leaving, and the new one hasn't taken shape yet. Braidotti advises not rushing into a new rigid identity, but drawing up a "cartography" of the moment — describing where you are now and which forces are acting on you. Seen this way, confusion is not losing yourself but a sign that you are in the process of becoming.
confusion.practice: Write two lines: "Who I am ceasing to be: …" and "Who I may be becoming: …". You don't have to finish the second one.

fatigue.text: Tiredness and burnout are not weakness but a signal that you have been working at your limit for a long time. Rosi Braidotti writes about sustainability not as endless endurance but as the ability not to break down: every body has its thresholds, and respecting them is an ethical choice, not a defeat. She criticises contemporary "cognitive capitalism", which expects constant productivity, flexibility and self-improvement from people. Braidotti's affirmative ethics isn't about heroism or pushing through at any cost. It's about preserving the strength to live and create by sharing the load and leaning on others. From this point of view, rest is not laziness but a way of staying in living connection with the world for the long haul.
fatigue.practice: What threshold do you feel in your body right now? What one thing could you remove or postpone today to stay within your strength?

boredom.text: Boredom seems like a small thing, but it can be oppressive. Braidotti doesn't write about boredom directly, but from the standpoint of her philosophy of becoming one could say this. For Braidotti, life is a continuous process of change and encounter, and a person is a knot of connections with a vast world, not only a human one. Boredom may arise when this flow narrows to a tight circle of familiar stimuli — a screen, a routine, the same old thoughts. The posthuman view invites you to widen your attention beyond the human: to notice birds, weather, plants, your own body, the technologies through which you live. The world is full of processes happening right now. In this light, boredom is not an absence of anything interesting but an invitation to reconnect with what is already living and changing around you.
boredom.practice: Look out of the window or step outside for a minute and find one non-human life to watch: a bird, a cloud, a leaf.

joy.text: Joy is no trifle — for Braidotti it is one of the most important forces of life. Following Spinoza, she understands joy as the experience of our capacity to act, feel and connect with the world increasing. Braidotti's affirmative ethics is built around such moments: they are not a naive escape from problems but a source of strength that helps us live and stand up to what is hard. Braidotti stresses that joy doesn't cancel pain or require us to forget it. It simply shows the direction in which life can grow. From this point of view, your joy is a valuable compass: it points to the encounters, activities and connections that make you stronger. You can not only live it but also remember it as a clue.
joy.practice: What exactly in this joy made you stronger or more alive? Write it down as a clue for the future.

love.text: Love and tenderness are encounters that change us. Rosi Braidotti, drawing on Spinoza and Deleuze, sees love above all as a mutual increase of power: a good connection makes both people more able to feel, think and live. Her nomadic view rejects love as possession: the other is not property and not the "other half" you were missing, but a living being on their own path, with whom you have fallen into step. Braidotti also extends love beyond the human: tenderness towards an animal, a place, the planet is no less real for her. From this point of view, your love is not a weakness or a dependency but one of the most powerful ways of becoming yourself together with others.
love.practice: What does this love make you more able to do — what can you feel or do thanks to it? Name one thing.

gratitude.text: Gratitude is a feeling in which we see that we don't live alone. Rosi Braidotti invites us to extend this thought to the scale of all life: we are not separate masters of the world but part of a vast web in which people, animals, plants, microorganisms, machines and the elements support one another. Braidotti calls this view "zoe-centred" — attention to life in all its forms, not only to the human. From this point of view, gratitude is the ability to notice countless supports: the tree that gives shade, the bees pollinating plants, people whose labour remains invisible. Such gratitude doesn't make us small; it makes us connected. And it reminds us that we, too, can be a support for others.
gratitude.practice: Silently thank one non-human form of life that supported you today — a plant, an animal, water.

hope.text: For Rosi Braidotti, hope is not a naive expectation that everything will sort itself out, but an active force. Her affirmative ethics faces the future: it invites us to think about what the world could become and to invest in that becoming right now. Braidotti draws on Deleuze's notion of the "virtual" — not the unreal, but the not-yet-actualised, what is ripening in the present as a possibility. From this point of view, hope is sensitivity to the virtual, to what may grow out of present connections. Braidotti stresses that such a future is built together, not alone. So your hope doesn't have to be certainty about the outcome. It can simply be a readiness to take part in what is only just being born.
hope.practice: What possibility, however small, is already ripening in your life? How could you support it with one action?

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is a tender longing for the past, and there is nothing shameful in it. Admittedly, Rosi Braidotti is wary of nostalgia as a social stance: longing for the "good old days" and for the old image of the human as master of the world, in her view, keeps us from seeing the present. But in personal memory she finds another possibility too. Following Deleuze, Braidotti understands memory not as an archive you can return to but as a creative force: in remembering, we reassemble the past anew and discover in it the seeds of the future. From this point of view, one could say that nostalgia is not only a backward glance. What you loved then can become a resource for who you are becoming now.
nostalgia.practice: Recall something you miss. What in it — a quality, a feeling, a habit — could you bring with you into today?

craving.text: A sharp "I want it right now" can feel like a wave that takes over your whole body, and there's no need to be ashamed of it. Rosi Braidotti, following Spinoza and Deleuze, asks of every urge not "is this good or bad?" but "how much can a body bear?". She speaks of "thresholds of sustainability": everyone has a limit beyond which what seems to add life begins to take it away. Braidotti is wary of romanticising "going beyond the limits" and insists that only experience that can be sustained and prolonged without destroying yourself is valuable. From this point of view, a craving is not a vice but a force seeking an outlet — one that, in this form, drains you. You don't have to suppress it or act on it at once; you can watch it: the wave rises, peaks and subsides. And you remain.
craving.practice: When the craving comes, rate its strength on a scale from 1 to 10. Five minutes later, rate it again — just to see how the wave moves.

addiction.text: When life has long been organised around one thing, it isn't a moral failure but a circle that is hard to break. Braidotti distinguishes two senses of power: potestas — power that restricts and captures — and potentia — the capacity to act, connect, grow. From this point of view, addiction can be described as a situation in which one connection gradually crowds out all the others and narrows potentia to a single tight channel. Braidotti offers neither condemnation nor a heroic leap. Her affirmative ethics is a slow, shared transformation of a draining force into a sustaining one: adding connections, not just taking away the habit. For her the subject is nomadic, always in motion — so no circle is your final essence.
addiction.practice: Name one small connection — with a person, a place, an activity — that gives you strength at no cost. Could you give it five minutes today? If you'd like, a mutual-help group can become such a connection too.

hangover.text: The morning after can be hard on every level: the body aches, and thoughts about yesterday bring anxiety and shame. Braidotti insists that we are "embodied and embedded" subjects: not a mind that happens to be placed in a body, but the body itself, bound up with its surroundings. That's why the physical and the moral hangover are intertwined: the body is depleted, and thoughts take on the darkest colours. From this point of view, the first step is not to judge yesterday but to care for the body: rest, fresh air, quiet. Braidotti speaks of "thresholds of sustainability" — how much a body can bear. A hangover can be understood as a message about such a threshold, not as proof that something is wrong with you. Sorting out yesterday is better left for later, when your strength returns.
hangover.practice: Do one thing right now just for your body — open a window, wash your face, lie down. Tell yourself: "Body first, thoughts later."

euphoria.text: A burst of elation, when everything seems possible, is the force of life in a very vivid form, and there's no need to be suspicious of it right away. Braidotti calls the impersonal force shared by all living things zoe — life in its excessive, creative surge, flowing through people, animals, plants. In euphoria we seem to feel this flow directly. Following Spinoza, Braidotti values joy as an affect that increases potentia — the capacity to act and connect with the world. But she also reminds us of thresholds of sustainability: a force is good when it can be sustained and prolonged. From this point of view, you can live and enjoy euphoria while also noticing which connections and ideas it has lit up — they may outlast the burst itself.
euphoria.practice: Write down one connection or one idea that this joy made brighter. Come back to the note in a week.

crash.text: A sharp drop after a high can be agonising: it's as if all your energy has been pumped out of you. Braidotti describes life as a flow of forces that swells and ebbs, and the body has its own "thresholds of sustainability". After an intense high — a celebration, a success, a turbulent event — comes a comedown, because energy isn't infinite. From this point of view, the crash is not a punishment and not a sign that the joy was fake, but the rhythm of a living body that needs to recover. Braidotti's affirmative ethics doesn't ask you to stay at the peak: it teaches you to build up strength slowly, leaning on your connections with other people and with the world. You can give yourself time: the comedown is also part of the movement, not its end.
crash.practice: Name one thing that slowly and quietly gives you your strength back — sleep, a walk, someone's voice. Make room for it today.

panic.text: A wave of panic is frightening: your heart pounds, your breath falters, it feels as though disaster is about to strike. Usually such a wave peaks and subsides within a few minutes. Braidotti, following Spinoza, thinks of a person as a body through which intense forces pass — and sometimes their flow becomes too strong. For her, we are not separate fortresses but beings "embedded" in the world: we are held by the ground, the air, objects, other living things. From this point of view, in a moment of panic you can lean on exactly these connections — not on the mind that is trying to explain everything immediately, but on what physically surrounds you. The wave passes through the body, but the body stays connected to the world that holds it.
panic.practice: Feel the floor holding your feet, and make your out-breath longer than your in-breath. Name five things you can see around you.

dread.text: Existential dread — "what is all this for?", the thought of finitude — can come over you with tremendous force. Braidotti doesn't brush this question aside, but she invites you to look at life more broadly than the life of a single self. She speaks of zoe — the impersonal force of life that flows through all living things and belongs to no one in particular. We are not owners of life but participants in it, connected to countless other beings — those who came before us and those who will come after. From this point of view, meaning isn't hidden somewhere outside the world, and it doesn't have to be proven: it takes shape in connections, in how you affect others and others affect you. Braidotti's affirmative ethics is not a once-and-for-all answer to the abyss, but daily care for what is alive now, together with others.
dread.practice: Name three living connections you are part of right now — a person, an animal, a plant, a place. Stay with them in your mind for a while.

fomo.text: The feeling that everyone else is living more vividly and you're not where you should be is a very familiar pain of our time. Braidotti describes contemporary capitalism as a system that speeds everything up and turns desires and attention into commodities. From this point of view, one could say that the social media feed is part of that machine: it sells an image of a life in which something is always happening, and it keeps fuelling a sense of lack. The fear of missing out isn't your personal flaw but an effect of a system that profits from restlessness. Braidotti proposes "cartography" — a careful description of where you actually are: which people, places and activities you are connected to. Such a map is usually richer than it seems when you're looking at other people's shop windows.
fomo.practice: Draw a small map of your "here": you in the centre, and around you the people, places and activities you are connected to right now.

sleepless.text: At night, when you can't sleep, thoughts run in circles and the world seems empty and quiet. Braidotti reminds us that we are bodily beings embedded in the rhythms of the world: day and night, light and darkness, work and rest. From her point of view, one could say that modern life increasingly blurs these rhythms — screens, work without boundaries, constant availability. Then insomnia is tied not only to personal worries but also to a world that doesn't let the body stop in time. You don't have to turn it into yet another task that must be solved urgently. Braidotti emphasises our connection with the non-human world — with air, silence, breath. At three in the morning these connections haven't gone anywhere. You can simply be with them, without demanding sleep of yourself.
sleepless.practice: Listen to the sounds of the night — the wind, the house, your breathing — and name them to yourself without judging.

betrayal.text: Betrayal wounds you where you were open, and that pain deserves acknowledgement. Braidotti thinks of the human being as a nomadic subject woven from connections: we don't exist apart from those we love and trust. That's why betrayal feels like a tear in the very fabric you are made of. Braidotti doesn't demand that you quickly forgive or "let go". Her affirmative ethics is slow work: pain and anger are acknowledged, and then gradually, together with others, transformed from a destructive force into one that lets you go on living. From this point of view, betrayal doesn't cancel your capacity for connection; it shows which connection turned out to be fragile. The web that holds you is wider than one person — and you can see it anew.
betrayal.practice: Name three connections that held and stayed with you despite this wound.

jealousy.text: Jealousy seizes both body and mind: you want to hold on, to control, not to lose. Braidotti distinguishes potestas — power that wants to possess and fix in place — from potentia — a force that grows through connection. From this point of view, jealousy can be understood as a moment when love, which was potentia, starts reaching towards potestas: to hold on to the other, to fix them in one form. Braidotti doesn't shame you for this: fear of loss is the natural reaction of a being who treasures a connection. But her nomadic thinking reminds us that both you and the other are always in motion. Love that doesn't try to stop that motion becomes stronger. You might ask yourself: what would help me feel safe without holding on to the other by force?
jealousy.practice: Finish the sentence: "I would feel calmer if I myself…" — and find the part that depends on you, not on the other person.

resentment.text: Long-held resentment is heavy: you carry it with you for years, and it wears down your strength. Braidotti, following Spinoza and Nietzsche, distinguishes affects that increase our capacity to act from those that decrease it. Nietzsche called long-festering grievance ressentiment — a pain that returns you to the past again and again, binding you to the moment when harm was done. Braidotti doesn't ask you to pretend the harm didn't happen. Her affirmative ethics isn't forgetting but slow transformation: turning passive pain into an active force that opens up the future. From this point of view, your resentment holds a truth, but it doesn't have to define your whole life. Such transformation doesn't happen on command — it's a process in which the support of others matters a great deal.
resentment.practice: Ask yourself: what would I spend the strength that now goes into this resentment on? Write down one wish.

heartbreak.text: A broken heart hurts on every level — in the body and in your thoughts about the future. Braidotti says we are nomadic subjects: our self is made up of connections, and when one of the most important ones breaks, we lose a part of ourselves. That's why a breakup is so disorienting. But being nomadic also means something else: you were never a frozen portrait; you are always in the process of becoming. In Metamorphoses Braidotti describes change not as a comforting formula but as the very fabric of life: experience, including painful experience, changes us. From this point of view, a breakup is not the end of your story but a painful turn in a movement that continues. The love you lived remains part of the strength you carry forward.
heartbreak.practice: Write down one thing this relationship taught you — a skill, a habit, a way of seeing. It stays with you.

impostor.text: The feeling that you're here by accident and are about to be found out is exhausting. Braidotti shows that the image of the "real", competent person is largely built on the old humanist ideal: a confident, self-sufficient, rational subject without doubts. But this ideal, for Braidotti, is a historical construction, not a description of real people. The nomadic subject is never final — it is always learning, changing, on the way. From this point of view, your sense that "I'm not quite in my place yet" is not an exposure but an honest feeling of movement. No one arrives at a point of final competence. Your doubts are a sign that you are growing, not frozen in a role.
impostor.practice: Compare yourself not with an imaginary "real expert" but with yourself a year ago. Write down one thing you have learned since then.

self_hatred.text: The inner critic can sound so sure of itself that it seems like the voice of truth. From the point of view of Braidotti, who follows Spinoza here, self-hatred is an affect that diminishes our potentia, our capacity to act and connect with the world. Such affects bring no knowledge about ourselves — they only drain us. Braidotti stresses that affirmative ethics is neither positive thinking nor an order to love yourself immediately. It is a slow transformation: step by step, ceasing to believe the forces that devalue life and leaning on the forces that sustain it. Seen this way, the critic isn't telling the truth about you; it speaks the language of norms that demand you be someone else. You are more than that voice: you are a multitude of connections, holding both worth and care.
self_hatred.practice: Recall one connection in which you were needed or useful to someone — a person, an animal, a cause. Write it down next to the critic's phrase.

helplessness.text: Feeling powerless to change anything is one of the heaviest feelings, and it often reflects real constraints. Braidotti distinguishes potestas — power that restricts and suppresses — from potentia — the capacity to act that every living being has. When potestas presses down, it seems that no potentia is left at all. But Braidotti insists that potentia is by its nature bound up with others: it grows in relationships. Where one person can't manage, many together can. From this point of view, helplessness speaks of the limits of your solitary effort, not the limits of life. Affirmative ethics begins small: find one connection that adds strength, and lean on it.
helplessness.practice: Name one connection that is giving you even a little strength right now. How could you reach out to it today?

procrastination.text: "I can't get started" is a state that easily turns into self-blame. Braidotti describes contemporary "cognitive capitalism" — an economy in which knowledge, attention and creative energy become the main resources — as a system that demands constant productivity and readiness. This pressure feels like personal responsibility, although it is largely systemic. From this point of view, one could say that procrastination is sometimes a signal about a threshold of sustainability: body and mind are saying "too much". Braidotti suggests asking not "why am I being lazy?" but "what right now increases my capacity to act, and what drains it?". Getting started is often easier not through forcing yourself, but through connection — with curiosity, with another person, with a small part of the task that resonates with you.
procrastination.practice: Find one small part of the task that interests you even slightly, and start with exactly that — for five minutes.

uprooted.text: Emigration or moving can feel like losing the ground beneath your feet, and this pain is real. Braidotti — born in Italy, raised in Australia, educated in France and working in the Netherlands — made the figure of the nomad central to her philosophy. The nomadic subject is not a homeless person, and not necessarily even a traveller, but someone who learns to live in motion without losing connections. For her, nomadism is not an absence of roots but a different relationship to them: roots become mobile and interwoven, like a web. Braidotti also writes about life between languages as a distinctive, rich experience. From this point of view, your uprootedness is not only a loss but also the beginning of a new map on which old and new connections intertwine. Your former home doesn't disappear: it becomes part of who you are becoming along the way.
uprooted.practice: Name one thing you brought with you from your former home — an object, a recipe, a word — and one thing you have found here.

quote.text: The nomadic subject is a myth, that is to say a political fiction, that allows me to think through and move across established categories and levels of experience.
quote.author: Rosi Braidotti

overload.text: The endless feed, notifications, news — all of it can overload you to the limit. Braidotti describes our era as "posthuman": we are constantly connected to technologies, networks, data flows, and the boundary between us and machines is growing ever thinner. She doesn't call for giving up technology, but she asks a Spinozist question: how much can a body bear? Today many people run up against their "thresholds of sustainability" because the flow of information grows faster than our capacity to take it in. From this point of view, overload isn't your inability to "cope" but a signal that a threshold has been reached. Braidotti reminds us that we are "embodied and embedded" beings. Returning to the body and the space around you is not escapism but a way of restoring your strength.
overload.practice: Put the screen aside and for one minute listen only to the sounds of the room. Notice where in your body things have become a little quieter.

unreality.text: The feeling that the world, or you yourself, isn't quite real can be frightening, and it's worth speaking about gently. Braidotti doesn't write about this experience directly, but from her point of view one could say this: reality is felt through the body and through connections. She insists that we are "embodied and embedded" subjects: not an abstract mind hovering above the world, but bodies rooted in a specific place, time and environment. When life becomes too tense or too screen-bound, this rootedness can weaken. From this point of view, the return of reality begins with simple things: feeling your feet on the floor, touching an object, hearing a sound outside the window. These connections haven't gone anywhere — they have just grown quieter.
unreality.practice: Touch three different surfaces near you — fabric, wood, glass — and notice how they differ.

awe.text: Awe before something vast or beautiful — mountains, a starry sky, music — is one of the deepest experiences. From Braidotti's point of view, in such awe you can sense zoe — the impersonal force of life that flows through everything alive, from a human to a tree to a microbe. Her posthumanism invites you to see yourself not as the crown of creation but as part of an enormous web of life. In awe this thought becomes tangible: you are a small part and, at the same time, connected to something greater. This doesn't diminish you; it frees you from the need to be the centre of the world. Braidotti values affects that widen our connection with the world, and awe is one of the most powerful. You can simply live it, let it in and allow it to change the way you see.
awe.practice: Stay for a minute with whatever filled you with awe, and silently name one living being with whom you are sharing this world right now.

relief.text: Relief is when what was pressing on you finally lets go, and the body relaxes. Braidotti, following Spinoza, sees in such moments the return of potentia — our capacity to act and connect with the world. While we were under pressure, this force was compressed; now it can flow again. From this point of view, relief is not merely the absence of something bad but an affirmative affect worth noticing and feeling fully. Braidotti's affirmative ethics isn't about constantly waiting for new troubles but about paying attention to what increases life. Relief is exactly such a moment. You can give yourself time to feel your strength returning, and not rush to load it with new tasks straight away.
relief.practice: Stretch your whole body and notice where the strength is coming back. Give yourself a few more minutes without new tasks.

calm.text: Calm and peace are rare states in a world that keeps speeding up. Braidotti describes advanced capitalism as a system in which everything moves faster and demands constant reaction from us. Against this background, calm is almost a form of resistance, a way of keeping your own rhythm. From Braidotti's point of view, one could say that calm is not passivity but a time when strength accumulates and is restored, when the body lives in harmony with its thresholds of sustainability. In calm it's easier to feel your connection with the slow rhythms of the world — breathing, the passing of the day, the growth of plants. Nomadic thought doesn't set movement against rest: even a nomad stops for the night. Allow yourself this stop — it is part of the journey.
calm.practice: Find something nearby that lives slowly — a plant, the clouds, light on the wall — and watch it for a minute.

inspiration.text: Inspiration is the feeling that a current is flowing through you and you want to create. For Braidotti, creativity never belongs to a single self: we are nomadic subjects through whom forces, ideas and influences pass — from other people, books, places and even non-human beings. From this point of view, inspiration is a moment when these currents are especially tangible and you become their conduit. Braidotti, following Deleuze, speaks of "becoming" — a process in which we are constantly turning into something new. Inspiration is becoming, experienced from within. You can cherish it without clinging to it or demanding an immediate result. Even if the current ebbs, its trace will remain in you as a grown capacity to see and create.
inspiration.practice: Write down which people, places or beings "passed through you" in this idea. Thank them, even if only silently.

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude is an unpleasant discovery about yourself, but a very human one. Braidotti, following Spinoza, distinguishes two forms of power: potentia — our own capacity to live and act — and potestas, power structured as hierarchy and comparison. Schadenfreude usually flares up where we are living inside the logic of potestas: someone is higher, someone lower, and another person's fall seems to lift us up a step. From her point of view, one could say that this feeling speaks not of your "corrupt nature" but of how deeply competition is built into us. Joy at someone else's failure doesn't add to your strength — it only shifts your place on the ladder for a moment. Noticing this is already a step towards a different joy, one that grows out of your own strength rather than someone else's weakness.
schadenfreude.practice: Ask yourself: what in me felt a moment of relief at someone else's failure? What am I myself lacking right now?

contempt.text: Contempt gives a sense of clarity and superiority, and sometimes it protects us from something that hurts too much. Braidotti writes a great deal about how classical humanism built the image of the "real human" through disdain for "others": women, strangers, animals, everything bodily. For her, contempt is one of the ways of drawing an "us and them" line and freezing on one side of it. Her idea of the nomadic subject offers something else: you are not a fortress but a moving knot of connections, and what you despise is often more closely tied to you than you'd like to think. From this point of view, contempt doesn't need to be uprooted by force. You can explore it like a map: where does the boundary I'm guarding run? What does it protect in me — and hasn't it become too narrow?
contempt.practice: Name in one word what exactly you despise in this person or phenomenon. Then ask: what does this boundary protect in me?

disgust.text: Disgust is an ancient, bodily feeling: it makes us recoil before we have time to think. Braidotti insists that we are "embodied and embedded" beings: thought is not separate from the body, nor the body from its environment. So for her, disgust is not a whim but a reaction of the whole organism, one worth respecting. But she also shows that culture often teaches disgust: towards bodiliness, old age, the "unclean", other kinds of living beings. From her point of view, one could say that part of your disgust really does protect you, while part of it is a learned boundary. And if it is turned on yourself, it's important to remember: your body is not a mistake but a stretch of the same life that Braidotti calls by the Greek word zoe — the impersonal, stubborn force of the living, shared by all.
disgust.practice: Notice where in your body the disgust resonates. Ask: is this protecting me right now — or is it an old rule I was taught?

revenge.text: The desire for revenge is a natural response to pain that has been inflicted, and there is nothing shameful in the desire itself. Braidotti, following Nietzsche and Deleuze, would call it a "reactive" force: it is entirely defined by whoever hurt us and ties us to them again and again. Revenge promises to restore the balance, but in fact it makes the offender the centre of our life. Braidotti's affirmative ethics suggests neither suppressing this energy nor being ashamed of it, but slowly recasting negative affects into a force that works for life. From this point of view, the wish for revenge shows how important the thing that was hurt really was. The same force can become self-protection, recovery, new boundaries — and you will stop revolving around the person who caused the pain.
revenge.practice: Write down what exactly was hurt — dignity, trust, safety. What could restore it without involving the offender at all?

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at the people close to us comes precisely because they are close: the tighter the bond, the more friction in it. For Braidotti, the subject is not a closed-off self but a web of relations; we are literally woven from those we live with. That's why in closeness it isn't only feelings that collide, but also rhythms, needs and limits of endurance. Braidotti speaks of "thresholds of sustainability" — the limits up to which we can bear tension without breaking down. Anger at a partner, parent or child often means that such a threshold has been reached, not that you love badly. From this point of view, there's no need to be ashamed of the feeling itself. What matters more is noticing what you're short of — rest, help, space of your own — and taking care of it, without unleashing that force on the people around you.
anger_at_loved.practice: When anger rises, ask yourself: which of my limits has just been crossed? What one small thing could widen it a little?

ambivalence.text: Loving someone and not being able to stand them at the same time is not a contradiction that has to be resolved urgently, but the ordinary fabric of closeness. Braidotti thinks along with Deleuze: the subject is not a solid monolith but a multiplicity in which different forces act at once. The nomadic, wandering self doesn't have to hold one final attitude towards a person; it passes through different states, like a traveller through different landscapes. From this point of view, your mixed feelings are an honest reflection of the fact that the relationship is alive and complex: it holds both what strengthens you and what drains you. You don't need to decide which feeling is the "real" one. You can map them instead — Braidotti is fond of the word "cartography": noting what exactly in this connection gives you strength and what takes it away.
ambivalence.practice: Divide a sheet of paper into two columns: "what in this relationship gives me strength" and "what takes it away". Just fill them in, without drawing conclusions.

guilty_relief.text: Relief you feel ashamed of is one of the quietest and loneliest feelings. It can come after a breakup, after leaving a job, after a long time caring for a seriously ill loved one. Braidotti, drawing on Spinoza, sees us as beings of limited endurance: each of us can bear strain only up to a certain threshold, and prolonged strain drains potentia — the power to live and act. When it ends, body and soul straighten up. That is what relief is, and it doesn't cancel your love. From Braidotti's point of view, one could say that love and relief belong to different layers of one life and can sit side by side perfectly well. Relief is not betrayal but a sign of how hard it was for you. You can allow it to be, the way you let yourself exhale after holding your breath for a long time.
guilty_relief.practice: Tell yourself, out loud if you like: "I loved — and it was very hard for me. Both of these truths are real."

indifference.text: Sometimes something ought to move you, and inside it's quiet. This is frightening, but it happens to many people. Braidotti describes our time as a stream of alarming news, crises and demands to which no one can keep responding with their whole heart forever. She speaks of "sustainability" not as heroic endurance but as the search for a rhythm of life that can actually be sustained. From this point of view, indifference can be understood as a protective lowering of sensitivity once a threshold has already been crossed, rather than as callousness. What's more, for Braidotti, affects don't belong to us alone — they are born in connections. When connections are depleted, the response grows quiet. You can give it time to return through what is small, near and bodily, rather than by demanding that you immediately feel "the way you should".
indifference.practice: Find one small thing that stirs even a faint response in you today — a smell, a sound, a touch. Stay with it for a minute.

escape.text: The urge to drop everything and leave — a job, a city, a role — is familiar to a great many people. Braidotti made the image of the nomad central to her philosophy. But her "nomadism" isn't necessarily a physical move: it is the ability not to freeze in a single identity, to keep moving, to cross boundaries within yourself. From her point of view, the wish to escape may be a signal that a role has become too tight, that you have outgrown some form of life. It isn't weakness or irresponsibility but the voice of your capacity for movement. You don't have to decide anything big right away. You can start with a small nomadic step — change a route, a habit, the people you spend time with — and sense where you are really being drawn: away from something, or towards something new.
escape.practice: Finish two sentences: "I want to get away from…" and "I want to move towards…". Notice which one comes more easily.

forbidden_attraction.text: Attraction to someone who is "off limits" can be confusing and unsettling. Braidotti, following Spinoza and Deleuze, understands desire not as lack but as a creative force — a striving for connection, for the expansion of life. In her view, desire is always bigger than a single person: through someone specific we are drawn towards a particular quality, possibility, way of being. From this point of view, one could say that such an attraction tells you something about yourself — about what kind of life, or what part of yourself, you are missing right now. It demands neither immediate action nor a verdict. You can look at it as a map of your forces: what exactly draws you so strongly to this person? And what place could that quality take in your own life?
forbidden_attraction.practice: Write down three words about what draws you to this person. Which of these qualities would you like more of in yourself or in your life?

social_anxiety.text: Shyness and the fear of being judged turn an ordinary conversation into an ordeal. Braidotti shows that behind the fear of "not measuring up" there is often an invisible norm — the image of a confident, talkative person who always knows the right thing to say. This image, like the classical ideal of the Vitruvian Man, is not universal at all: it passes off one way of being as the yardstick for everyone. Braidotti's nomadic subject doesn't have to match the norm; difference is not a defect but a way of living. Besides, in her view, we are connected to others not only by words but also by presence, attention and bodily closeness. From this point of view, you don't need to be a brilliant conversationalist to truly take part. Quiet attention is also a connection. Perhaps someone near you is feeling exactly the same.
social_anxiety.practice: At your next gathering, set yourself one goal — to listen closely to one person. You don't need to say anything brilliant.

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty is tiring: you want to know what you can rely on. Braidotti describes our time as an era of deep transitions — technological, ecological, social — when many familiar landmarks are shaken. She doesn't promise certainty. But her nomadic subject lives in motion from the start: it doesn't look for a final point of support but learns to find its way as it goes. Braidotti calls this a "cartography of the present" — the ability to map what is happening now without the illusion that the whole road is known in advance. From this point of view, uncertainty is not a sign that you're lost but the ordinary condition of being on the way. You can lean not on knowledge of the future but on connections: the people, habits and places that hold you here and now.
uncertainty.practice: Draw a small "map of the present": three sources of support you have today — people, places, activities.

waiting.text: Waiting drags on: it's as if life has been put on pause until the answer comes. Braidotti thinks of time not as an empty line between events but as continuous becoming: at every moment something is happening, even when it seems nothing is. Life, which she calls zoe, doesn't stop — the body breathes, connections go on, the world around you changes. From this point of view, one could say that waiting doesn't have to be an empty gap between "before" and "after". It is also part of your life, with its own sounds, people and small tasks. You don't have to force yourself not to think about the outcome. You can wait and, at the same time, notice that life is going on right now — and the pause becomes a little less empty.
waiting.practice: While you wait, see one simple task through to the end — water a plant, make some tea — and note: this has already happened.

regret.text: Regret — for what you did or didn't do — keeps returning you to crossroads that are already behind you. Braidotti, following Deleuze, understands the human being not as an unchanging essence but as a process of becoming. The person who made that choice is you, and yet not quite you: you have changed since then, in many ways thanks to that very choice. The idea of "transformation" is close to her heart: the pain of the past isn't erased, but it can become material for new connections and new strength. From this point of view, regret is a sign of what matters to you and of the fact that you keep changing. The past can't be rewritten, but you can influence what it becomes in the rest of your life: a lesson, care for someone, a different choice in a similar situation.
regret.practice: Write one sentence: what has this regret taught me about what I truly value?

longing.text: Longing for a particular person is the weight of their absence, felt almost physically. Braidotti holds that we are made of connections: another person is not an external object but part of how you live, feel and think. So when they aren't around, it feels as though a piece of you is missing. From Braidotti's point of view, one could say that this isn't weakness but evidence of how real the connection was. And it doesn't vanish entirely — what this person gave you lives on in your habits, words and tastes. Her ethics suggests not freezing in the pain but letting the connection continue in new forms: through memory, gratitude and what you pass on.
longing.practice: Recall one habit or phrase you picked up from this person. Let yourself use it today.

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — wars, injustice, heavy news — can sometimes feel unbearable. Braidotti puts it like this: we are all in this together, but we are not one and the same. We are connected to other people, to animals and to the whole planet, which is why others' pain echoes in us; it is a sign of living connection, not weakness. But Braidotti also warns that it is impossible to bear everything alone. Her affirmative ethics is not naive optimism but a decision to keep living and acting together with others despite the pain, and to protect your own strength so as not to burn out. From this point of view, you are not obliged to hold all the grief of the world inside you. You can choose one thread — one cause, one person, one community — and hold on to it.
world_pain.practice: Try spending less time on the news today, and instead do one small kind thing for a specific person near you.

rejection.text: Rejection wounds deeply: it feels as though it wasn't an offer that was rejected, but you as a whole. Braidotti describes the human being as a nomadic subject — not a finished portrait but a process, a multitude of connections and possibilities. One encounter, one form of connection can be rejected, but not the whole of that movement at once. Moreover, in her view any connection depends on both sides, on their strength, circumstances and timing; the fact that it didn't come together is not a verdict on one person. From this point of view, one could say that rejection means this connection didn't happen right now — it says nothing about your worth. The pain is honest, and it deserves to be lived through. But your capacity to form connections hasn't gone anywhere — it is simply looking for another direction.
rejection.practice: List three connections in your life where you are accepted as you are — even very small ones.

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned can be very old, almost childlike — and no less real for that. Braidotti emphasises that we are relational beings, and our vulnerability is tied precisely to this. We are not the autonomous fortresses that classical humanism painted us as; we depend on one another. From her point of view, this is not a flaw but a shared condition of life, and the fear of losing someone only shows how important that person is. But Braidotti also hints at a way out of the vicious circle: the nomadic subject holds on not to one thread but to many. The more varied your connections — with people, activities, places — the less any single possible loss feels like the end of everything. The fear doesn't disappear, but your support grows wider.
abandonment.practice: Name five threads that support you apart from this person: people, activities, places, animals.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love is a strong feeling with nowhere to go. Braidotti, following Spinoza, sees love not as lack but as a rise in power — joy connected with the image of another person. Even without a response, this force is real: it has changed you, made you more sensitive, opened up something new. From her point of view, one could say that love doesn't have to be an exchange to be meaningful. The other side of the connection didn't respond — that hurts, and it needs to be acknowledged. But the capacity to love that you have discovered in yourself remains yours. Braidotti's affirmative ethics suggests neither renouncing this force nor blaming yourself for it, but gradually letting it flow in other directions too — towards people, activities, yourself.
unrequited.practice: Write down what this love has opened up in you: what quality, sensitivity or desire you have discovered in yourself.

humiliation.text: Humiliation is the feeling of being thrown down while everyone watched. Braidotti distinguishes two forms of power: potestas — power that places some above others — and potentia — the inner capacity to live and act. Humiliation is an act of potestas: someone uses a hierarchy to make you smaller. But from her point of view, potestas can wound your position without cancelling your potentia. Your capacity to feel, to connect with others, to act stays with you. Braidotti describes affirmative ethics as a slow, shared process of recovering strength. So you don't have to "swallow" humiliation alone. You can tell someone who is on your side about it — that brings back the sense that you are not alone and not "down below".
humiliation.practice: Ask yourself: who in this situation was using power? Write: "This was about their power, not about my worth."

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body is familiar to almost everyone — and it often speaks in someone else's voice. Braidotti shows that the ideal of the "proper body" has been historically constructed: the classical image of the human — young, male, healthy, symmetrical — served as the measure by which everything else was deemed a deviation. Contemporary culture has merely swapped the standards. Braidotti's posthuman view sees the body differently: not as a façade to be adjusted to a norm, but as a living process, a knot of forces and connections, part of zoe — the life shared by all living things. From this point of view, your body is not a project that failed but that with which you feel, move and embrace. You can shift your attention, even briefly, from how it looks to what it does.
body_shame.practice: Name three things your body has done for you today — even the simplest ones.

illness.text: When your body lets you down, the world shrinks, and fear, anger and tiredness in this situation are entirely understandable. Braidotti insists that we are "embodied" beings: thought and feeling are inseparable from the body with its rhythms and limits. Classical humanism dreamed of the human as the sovereign master of their body; Braidotti considers this dream an illusion. For her, the body is not a machine that has "broken" but a living process with its own logic, and vulnerability is a shared condition of all living beings. From this point of view, one could say that illness doesn't make you "less of a person". It changes your rhythm and your connections, and within this new rhythm, too, you can look for what sustains the strength to live — people, small things, moments of calm.
illness.practice: Notice one small act of care today — from another person or from yourself — and allow yourself to accept it.

pride.text: Pride in what you have done is a good, legitimate feeling, and it's worth allowing yourself. Braidotti, drawing on Spinoza, understands joy as a growth of potentia — our capacity to act. Pride in something seen through to the end is exactly that kind of joy: you have felt what you are capable of. Her affirmative ethics values such moments because they nourish life. At the same time, Braidotti stresses that we never act alone: behind every achievement there are connections — people, conditions, support, even tools. From this point of view, pride needs neither to be hidden nor inflated. It can be shared: you can rejoice in your own strength and notice those who helped. Pride like this doesn't wall you off from others; it connects you to them.
pride.practice: Write down what exactly you did, and one person or one thing that helped. Be glad about both.

melancholy.text: Gentle sadness is a quiet, pensive feeling that you don't want to chase away. Braidotti argued against the melancholic tone of contemporary critical thought — the habit of seeing in the world nothing but loss, decline and the end. But her quarrel is with the pose of hopelessness, not with the delicate sadness that makes us sensitive. From her point of view, one could say that melancholy can be a form of attention — to fragility, to what is passing, to the fact that everything alive is changeable and in the process of becoming. Such sadness doesn't take away the strength to live; it deepens your connection with the world. Affirmative ethics doesn't demand that you hurry to replace it with joy. It invites you to notice what tenderness towards the world this sadness carries within it, and to let it be part of your movement.
melancholy.practice: Name what exactly your gentle sadness is about. Write one sentence about what in it is dear to you.
